Purpose To compare physiological responses to submaximal cycling and sprint cycling performance in women using oral contraceptives (WomenOC) and naturally cycling women (WomenNC) and to determine whether N-acetylcysteine (NAC) supplementation mediates these responses. Methods Twenty recreationally trained women completed five exercise trials (i.e., an incremental cycling test, a familiarisation trial, a baseline performance trial and two double-blind crossover intervention trials). During the intervention trials participants supplemented with NAC or a placebo 1 h before exercise. Cardiopulmonary parameters and blood biochemistry were assessed during 40 min of fixed-intensity cycling at 105% of gas-exchange threshold and after 1-km cycling time-trial. Results WomenOC had higher ventilation ( β [95% CI] = 0.07 L·min −1 [0.01, 0.14]), malondialdehydes ( β = 12.00 mmol·L −1 [6.82, 17.17]) and C-reactive protein (1.53 mg·L −1 [0.76, 2.30]), whereas glutathione peroxidase was lower ( β = 22.62 mU·mL −1 [− 41.32, − 3.91]) compared to WomenNC during fixed-intensity cycling. Plasma thiols were higher at all timepoints after NAC ingestion compared to placebo, irrespective of group (all p < 0.001; d = 1.45 to 2.34). For WomenNC but not WomenOC, the exercise-induced increase in malondialdehyde observed in the placebo trial was blunted after NAC ingestion, with lower values at 40 min ( p = 0.018; d = 0.73). NAC did not affect cycling time-trial performance. Conclusions Blood biomarkers relating to oxidative stress and inflammation are elevated in WomenOC during exercise. There may be an increased strain on the endogenous antioxidant system during exercise, since NAC supplementation in WomenOC did not dampen the exercise-induced increase in malondialdehyde. Future investigations should explore the impact of elevated oxidative stress on exercise adaptations or recovery from exercise in WomenOC. Griffith University Open Access funding enabled and organized by CAUL and its Member Institutions issue-copyright-statement © Springer-Verlag GmbH Germany, part of Springer Nature 2022 Introduction Prolonged high-intensity exercise is one stimulus that transiently disrupts the pro-oxidant and antioxidant (i.e., redox) environment, often resulting in oxidative stress and damage (Powers and Jackson 2008 ; Thirupathi and Pinho 2018 ). While an acute increase in exercise-induced oxidative stress may be important for training adaptations (Gomez-Cabrera et al. 2008 ), excessive production of reactive oxygen and nitrogen species (RONS) during prolonged exercise has been associated with skeletal muscle fatigue (Barclay and Hansel 1991 ; Powers and Jackson 2008 ). Thus, exercise generated RONS can be described by a bell-shaped (hormesis) curve, whereby there are two endpoints of physiological function (Reid et al. 1993 ). Another factor that may moderate performance is the effect of oral contraceptives (OC) on the redox environment during exercise. Irrespective of training status, OC-use has been consistently associated with oxidative stress and damage measured at rest via blood biomarkers, e.g., elevated malondialdehyde (MDA) and low lipid-soluble antioxidants (Cauci et al. 2016 ; De Groote et al. 2009 ; Kowalska and Milnerowicz 2016 ; Palan et al. 2006 ; Quinn et al. 2018 ; Quinn et al. 2021 ). Therefore, it could be postulated that oxidative stress is exacerbated in women using OC compared to women naturally cycling during high-intensity exercise. This concurrent OC- and exercise-induced oxidative stress may drive a rightwards shift on the hormesis curve and affect skeletal muscle function and subsequent performance. However, there is paucity of experimental research in women, particularly research that controls for female sex hormones when investigating physiological responses to exercise. Although several studies have found that OC use increases oxidative stress at rest, only one study has examined the exercise-induced change in lipid peroxidation in women using OC (Massart et al. 2012 ). Massart et al. ( 2012 ) found that MDA significantly increased in both OC-users and non-users after a combat (Judo) training session, but the percent magnitude of change (i.e., pre- to post-exercise) was greater in OC non-users. However, the implications that this has on performance was not investigated (Massart et al. 2012 ), and tightly controlled research that accounts for relative work performed is required to clarify the influence of OC-use on exercise-induced oxidative stress. Characterising these physiological responses to exercise in more detail is important given that approximately 50% of female athletes use OC (Larsen et al. 2020b ). In an effort to understand the effect of RONS on skeletal muscle function, study designs have employed the use of antioxidant supplementation (Matuszczak et al. 2005 ; Paschalis et al. 2018 ). Associated findings suggest that when the concentration of exercise-generated RONS is high, the administered antioxidant may protect muscle cells against RONS-related fatiging mechanisms (e.g., calcium sensitivity) and thus enhance performance (Andrade et al. 2001 ; Matuszczak et al. 2005 ). One such antioxidant is N-acetylcysteine (NAC), which has been shown to protect cells against oxidative insults by acting as a cysteine donor for the (re)synthesis of glutathione, mitochondrial sulfane sulphur production and/or to a lesser extent, a direct scavenging ability (Aldini et al. 2018 ). In exercise physiology research conducted predominately in men, NAC has been established as an ergogenic aid in hand-grip exercise (Matuszczak et al. 2005 ), intermittent high-intensity running (Cobley et al. 2011 ; Rhodes et al. 2019 ) and high-intensity cycling exercise (McKenna et al. 2006 ; Medved et al. 2004b ; Paschalis et al. 2018 ; Slattery et al. 2014 ). More recently, the use of NAC as an ergogenic aid has been demonstrated to be more effective in male participants with a glutathione deficiency compared to those with normal or high glutathione levels (Margaritelis et al. 2020 ; Paschalis et al. 2018 ). As such, the available research suggests that NAC supplementation may have a positive impact on exercise performance for women using OC given there is preliminary evidence demonstrating low glutathione and glutathione peroxidase (GPx) in OC-users at rest (Kowalska and Milnerowicz 2016 ; Quinn et al. 2021 ). Our primary aim was to determine whether there are differences in blood biomarkers of oxidant damage and antioxidants during heavy, fixed-intensity exercise in women naturally cycling compared to women using OC. We were also interested in exploring whether acute (i.e., 1 h prior to exercise) NAC supplementation alters blood biomarkers during fixed-intensity cycling in the two groups, and whether there was any subsequent effect on 1-km cycling time trial (TT) performance. It was hypothesized that oxidant damage would change similarly for both groups in response to exercise; however, women using OC would have higher absolute oxidant damage measured in the blood after exercise compared to naturally cycling women. It was also hypothesized that NAC supplementation would dampen the increase in biomarkers of oxidant damage in both groups, however, improve cycling TT performance only in women using OC.

extracted_data.document_summary: This study investigated the influence of oral contraceptive (OC) use on physiological, oxidative stress, and inflammatory responses to fixed-intensity and sprint cycling in recreationally trained women, comparing them to naturally cycling women. It also examined the acute effects of N-acetylcysteine (NAC) supplementation on these responses and 1-km cycling time trial performance. Key findings showed that women using OC had elevated oxidative stress (higher MDA, lower GPx) and inflammation (higher CRP) biomarkers, as well as increased ventilation, during exercise. While NAC supplementation increased plasma thiols, it only blunted exercise-induced malondialdehyde increases in naturally cycling women, not in OC users, and did not improve cycling performance in either group. This suggests an increased strain on the endogenous antioxidant system in women using OC during exercise.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Acute N-acetylcysteine (NAC) supplementation and cycling exercise (fixed-intensity and sprint time trial).
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Twenty recreationally trained women completed five exercise trials, including two double-blind crossover intervention trials where participants acutely supplemented with NAC or a placebo. NAC was administered orally in a total dose of 105 mg·kg⁻¹ of body mass, given as 70 mg·kg⁻¹ 60 minutes prior to exercise and 35 mg·kg⁻¹ 30 minutes prior. The exercise protocol involved 40 minutes of fixed-intensity cycling at 105% of the gas-exchange threshold (GET), immediately followed by an all-out 1-km cycling time trial. No dose-response comparisons for NAC were reported beyond the acute vs. placebo comparison.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Increased during cycling (  = 0.10 L·min⁻¹ [0.04, 0.15]), with a greater magnitude of increase in WomenOC compared to WomenNC (  = 0.07 L·min⁻¹ [0.01, 0.14]), irrespective of supplementation.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Regulation of gas exchange and respiratory volume in response to metabolic demands.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: During fixed-intensity cycling, comparing women using oral contraceptives (WomenOC) to naturally cycling women (WomenNC).
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Higher ventilation in WomenOC suggests a heightened physiological response or altered cardiorespiratory efficiency during submaximal exercise, possibly related to their hormonal status.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Resting levels were significantly higher in WomenOC compared to WomenNC (  = 12.00 mmol·L⁻¹ [6.82, 17.17]). Exercise induced an increase in MDA (Time effect   = 13.47 mmol·L⁻¹ [4.10, 22.84]). In the placebo trial, MDA increased after 1-km cycling TT by +2.86 mmol·L⁻¹ (p = 0.036; d = 0.32) in WomenNC and +5.22 mmol·L⁻¹ (p < 0.001; d = 0.55) in WomenOC. Acute NAC supplementation attenuated this increase in WomenNC (lower by -3.28 mmol·L⁻¹ after 40-min cycling, p = 0.018; d = -0.73, and -3.69 mmol·L⁻¹ after 1-km TT, p = 0.017; d = -0.50) but had no attenuating effect on exercise-associated MDA increase in WomenOC.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: End-product of lipid peroxidation, indicative of oxidative damage to cell membranes.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Resting levels, during fixed-intensity cycling, and after 1-km cycling time trial, in naturally cycling women (WomenNC) and women using oral contraceptives (WomenOC), with or without acute N-acetylcysteine (NAC) supplementation.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Higher MDA indicates increased oxidative stress and cellular damage, particularly noted in WomenOC at rest and during exercise, suggesting a greater challenge for redox homeostasis. While NAC attenuated exercise-induced MDA increases in WomenNC, it had no such protective effect in WomenOC, potentially indicating OC-induced depletion of endogenous antioxidant capacity or a different redox status.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Resting levels were significantly higher in WomenOC compared to WomenNC (  = 1.53 mg·L⁻¹ [0.76, 2.30]). This higher level persisted during fixed-intensity cycling, with no significant effect of time or NAC supplementation.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: An acute-phase protein produced by the liver, acting as a non-specific marker of systemic inflammation.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Resting levels and during heavy fixed-intensity cycling, comparing women using oral contraceptives (WomenOC) to naturally cycling women (WomenNC).
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Elevated levels signify increased systemic inflammation, indicating a heightened baseline inflammatory state in WomenOC, possibly linked to oral contraceptive use, which can impact recovery and adaptation to exercise.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Lower GPx levels were observed at rest and during fixed-intensity cycling in WomenOC compared to WomenNC (  = -22.62 mU·mL⁻¹ [-41.32, -3.91]). No exercise-induced change in GPx was observed in either group.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: An enzyme critical for antioxidant defense, catalyzing the breakdown of hydroperoxides to water, thus protecting cells from oxidative damage.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Resting levels and during fixed-intensity cycling, in naturally cycling women (WomenNC) versus women using oral contraceptives (WomenOC).
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Lower GPx activity in WomenOC suggests a compromised endogenous antioxidant defense system and reduced antioxidant capacity, potentially indicating higher baseline oxidative stress and increased susceptibility to oxidative stress during exercise, possibly related to exogenous sex steroid use.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Plasma thiols were consistently higher at all timepoints after acute N-acetylcysteine (NAC) ingestion compared to placebo, irrespective of group (all p < 0.001; d = 1.45 to 2.34), and remained elevated during exercise. No between-group differences were observed in endogenous thiol levels.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Molecules containing a sulfhydryl (-SH) group, crucial for antioxidant defense and maintaining redox homeostasis as part of the non-enzymatic endogenous antioxidant defense system.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Following acute N-acetylcysteine (NAC) supplementation (1 hour prior to exercise) and during subsequent exercise.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Increased plasma thiols after acute NAC ingestion demonstrate effective absorption and bioavailability of NAC, indicating enhanced antioxidant capacity and altered blood redox status, crucial for defense against oxidative stress.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: lower in WomenOC; elevated in WomenNC (mid-luteal confirmation)
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Statistically lower in women using oral contraceptives (WomenOC) compared to naturally cycling women (WomenNC). In WomenNC, levels were confirmed as elevated (  16 nmol·L⁻¹) for mid-luteal phase verification.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Female sex-steroid hormone critical for regulating the menstrual cycle and reproductive functions.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Resting levels, used for mid-luteal phase confirmation in naturally cycling women (WomenNC), and for comparison with women using oral contraceptives (WomenOC).
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates hormonal status related to oral contraceptive use, and critical for characterizing the specific menstrual cycle phase in naturally cycling women to control for hormonal variability in physiological research.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: A positive test indicated, with a level of confidence of 95%, that ovulation would occur 14–26 h later.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Triggers ovulation and stimulates the production of progesterone and estrogen in the menstrual cycle.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Prediction of ovulation for accurate timing of experimental trials in WomenNC participants.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Critical for determining the precise testing window (mid-luteal phase) in naturally cycling women, which is essential for controlling hormonal variability and ensuring consistency in study conditions.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Statistically lower in WomenOC compared to WomenNC.

analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Resting levels, comparison between WomenOC and WomenNC.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates hormonal status related to oral contraceptive use.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Increased with time during fixed-intensity cycling. Not different between Supplement or Group. Peak heart rate for WomenNC during placebo 1-km TT was 187 beat·min⁻¹ [182, 192], during NAC 186 beat·min⁻¹ [181, 191]. For WomenOC during placebo 1-km TT was 185 beat·min⁻¹ [179, 190], during NAC 185 beat·min⁻¹ [180, 191]. Not statistically different between groups in placebo or NAC trial.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Indicator of cardiovascular effort and physiological response to exercise.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: During fixed-intensity cycling and 1-km cycling time trial.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Reflects cardiovascular demand during exercise, with no significant differences observed between groups or with NAC supplementation.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Increased with time (  = 0.003 L·min⁻¹ [0.002, 0.004]). Not different between Group or Supplement.

analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Reflects aerobic capacity and energy expenditure during exercise, with no significant differences observed between groups or with NAC supplementation.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Decreased over time (  = − 0.0024 [− 0.0029, − 0.0019]). Not different between Group or Supplement.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Indicator of substrate utilization (ratio of CO2 produced to O2 consumed).
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Reflects a shift towards increased fat oxidation during prolonged exercise, with no significant differences observed between groups or with NAC supplementation.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Measure of how effectively metabolic energy is converted into external work.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Preservation of efficiency with NAC suggests a potential benefit in sustaining performance during prolonged exercise, though the effect was marginal.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Increased during cycling (logit   = 0.017 [0.011, 0.023]). Not different between Group or Supplement.

analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: During fixed-intensity cycling and immediately post-exercise 1-km TT.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates the perceived intensity of exercise, with no significant differences observed between groups or with NAC supplementation.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Increased as a result of exercise, but not different between Ex 20 and Ex 40, or between Group or Supplement at any timepoint. For WomenNC, mean [95% CI] lactate at pre-exercise, Ex 20 and Ex 40 during placebo was 1.5 [0.8, 2.1], 3.3 [2.6, 3.9] and 3.1 [2.4, 3.8], respectively; and during NAC was 1.4 [0.7, 2.1], 3.2 [2.5, 3.8] and 3.0 [2.3, 3.7], respectively. analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Reflects the intensity of exercise and reliance on anaerobic energy pathways, with no significant differences observed between groups or with NAC supplementation.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Effect of Time (  = 3.43 mmol·L⁻¹, [1.38, 5.49]) and a Time by Supplement effect (  = − 3.09 mmol·L⁻¹ [− 6.04, − 0.14]). It was not clear whether TAC was statistically higher after the 1-km cycling TT (i.e., timepoint 'post') in the NAC trial compared to the placebo trial (p = 0.089; mean difference (MD) [95% CI] = 0.45 mmol·L⁻¹ [− 0.07, 0.97]; d = 0.36).

analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Higher TAC indicates better overall antioxidant defense. The unclear effect with NAC suggests limited or non-significant impact on overall antioxidant capacity in this context.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Statistically lower in the NAC trial compared to the placebo trial at the end of the 40-min cycling task (p = 0.005; MD = − 0.47 µmol·L⁻¹ [− 0.79, − 0.16]; d = − 0.40) and after the 1-km cycling TT (p < 0.001; MD = − 0.80 µmol·L⁻¹ [− 1.20, − 0.41]; d = − 1.01), irrespective of group. An effect of Time (  = 1.71 µmol·L⁻¹ [0.24, 3.16]), Supplement (  = − 0.29 µmol·L⁻¹ [− 0.56, − 0.02]), and a Time by Supplement interaction (  = -4.19 µmol·L⁻¹ [− 6.24, − 2.09]) were observed.

analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: During and after fixed-intensity cycling and 1-km cycling time trial, with acute N-acetylcysteine (NAC) or placebo supplementation.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Lower total glutathione during the NAC trial compared to placebo might suggest increased utilization during exercise or altered synthesis/breakdown pathways, requiring further investigation into reduced and oxidized glutathione levels for complete interpretation.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Showed an exercise-induced increase (Time effect   = 9.25 mol·L⁻¹ [2.78, 15.75]) after 40-min fixed-intensity cycling and 1-km cycling time trial compared to baseline in both groups. No significant differences were observed between groups at rest or during exercise, and no effect of NAC supplementation was found.

analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: During and after fixed-intensity cycling and 1-km cycling time trial, in naturally cycling women and women using oral contraceptives, with or without NAC supplementation.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates nitroxidative stress, which increased with exercise but was not significantly affected by OC use or NAC supplementation in this context.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Time effect (  time = 53.53 g·L⁻¹ [42.35, 64.72]), but no effect of Group or Supplement.
